When 3D Gaussian Splatting Recovers Real Surfaces

Songhe Wang Affiliation: School of EECS, Penn State, University Park, PA, USA E-mail {sxw5765,djm25}@psu.edu    David Miller Affiliation: School of EECS, Penn State, University Park, PA, USA E-mail {sxw5765,djm25}@psu.edu
Abstract

When does 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) recover the true scene surface rather than just overfitting view-dependent appearance? We answer this by developing a mathematical framework—based on a first-hit rendering abstraction—that cleanly isolates geometry from appearance. We prove that geometric misalignment forcefully converts spatial textures into high-frequency angular signals via parallax. This establishes a strict identifiability window: if angular capacity is bounded, surface-consistent solutions are mathematically preferred; if unrestricted, the same images can be perfectly explained by an incorrect, opaque “billboard” geometry. Experiments on synthetic stress tests confirm this prediction, showing billboard failures emerge precisely at high angular capacities. Conversely, in the real-world datasets we evaluate under standard capture protocols, reconstructions remain surface-consistent even at high SH degrees, which is consistent with the prediction that rich spatial texture can push billboard solutions outside the tested angular-capacity range.

Keywords: 
3D Gaussian Splatting Geometric Identifiability Spherical Harmonics Light Fields

1 Introduction

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) renders high-quality views in real time and has rapidly become a default primitive for 3D reconstruction and editing [20]. Crucially, modern pipelines no longer treat 3DGS as a hidden renderer that only produces images: they increasingly export the learned Gaussians as geometry and build downstream systems on top of them. On the one hand, a growing line of work treats 3DGS as a surrogate surface representation and demonstrates that high-quality triangle meshes can be extracted from learned Gaussian fields, making 3DGS a central building block for geometry processing and reconstruction [15, 41, 26, 42, 39, 7, 35, 40, 27, 43, 25, 2]. Across these lines of work, the learned Gaussian field is implicitly treated as if it were the true scene geometry: meshes are carved out of it, and downstream edits are applied on top of it. Yet all of this evidence is essentially empirical: to our knowledge there is no theoretical guarantee that the standard 3DGS objective actually recovers the underlying surface. Without such a guarantee, treating 3DGS as ground-truth geometry is methodologically fragile: a model that fits all training views while drifting off the true surface could silently corrupt downstream meshes and contact manifolds. This raises a basic question of geometric trustworthiness: under what conditions are the learned Gaussians truly surface-consistent, so that reconstruction and editing built on top of them rest on a sound geometric foundation? Here, surface-consistent means geometrically close to the true surface under nCD, not merely photometrically accurate.

In this work, we address this question from a theoretical point of view. We build a mathematical framework that isolates the interaction between a scene’s spatial geometry and its view-dependent appearance. Specifically, we abstract the rendering process to analyze the best-achievable population loss for any candidate surface under a bounded angular capacity—a strict limit on how complex the view-dependent colors are allowed to be. Within this framework, we demonstrate that optimizing appearance essentially reduces to a mathematical projection problem. This allows us to rigorously compare the approximation error of the true geometry against any misaligned geometry by evaluating their required angular frequencies.

Through this theoretical analysis, we predict a severe and counterintuitive vulnerability, which we refer to as the opaque billboard failure mode. Our proofs reveal that if the angular capacity is allowed to be excessively large, a geometrically misaligned surface can exploit high-frequency view-dependent colors to perfectly mimic the spatial details of the true background. In this regime, an artificial interior sheet can block the rays and paint the correct colors using high angular capacity, so the images look perfectly right even though the geometry is completely wrong (see Fig. 1). Conversely, our theory guarantees that if the angular capacity is appropriately restricted, the model is mathematically incapable of sustaining this illusion, ensuring the true geometry remains strictly easier to fit.

On the empirical side, we instantiate these theoretical predictions in practice. We construct a controlled synthetic stress-test dataset with tunable object complexity to deliberately probe this vulnerability. As predicted by our theoretical framework, training 3DGS with large angular capacity reliably triggers opaque billboard solutions: rendering quality remains near-optimal, while the geometry drifts completely off the true surface. In our real-scene benchmarks, the observed spatial texture complexity appears to push the induced frequency ωfake\omega_{\text{fake}} beyond the SH degrees we test (e.g., up to L=24L=24). Under these standard training setups and moderate capacities, we do not observe opaque billboard failures.

As a summary, our contributions are:

  • •

    We provide a mathematical framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that cleanly isolates geometry from appearance, turning the geometric identifiability problem into a rigorous frequency comparison.

  • •

    Within this framework, we mathematically predict the opaque billboard failure mode. We prove that given unbounded or large angular capacity, an incorrect surface can perfectly match training images by memorizing spatial textures as view-dependent signals.

  • •

    We establish a theoretical identifiability window, proving that strictly bounding angular capacity is mathematically necessary to reject billboards and guarantee accurate surface recovery.

  • •

    We complement the theory with controlled diagnostics, demonstrating that opaque billboard failures can be deterministically forced in synthetic stress tests, while no opaque-billboard cases appear in our real-scene diagnostics.

Scope.

Although framed around 3DGS, the mechanism applies to any proxy or surface representation with a finite-degree SH radiance head; 3DGS is our motivating instance.

2 Related Work

Meshes and downstream interactions in 3DGS.

Many methods extract surfaces from 3DGS using surface alignment [15, 41], 2D Gaussians or surfels [18, 9], SDFs [26, 42], geometric priors [39, 7], sparse adaptations [35, 40], or hybrid optimization [27], as surveyed in [43, 25, 2]. Others use Gaussians for dynamics, contact, and deformation [45, 13, 29, 19, 3, 16, 33, 37]. These applications rely on learned Gaussians as geometry, yet standard 3DGS [20] lacks surface-recovery guarantees.

Plenoptic bandwidth and spherical harmonics.

Classical studies in image-based rendering showed that view synthesis with imperfect proxy geometry converts spatial texture variation into angular variation, tying sampling requirements to depth and disparity [22, 14, 5, 24, 4, 11, 10, 30]. To model angular radiance efficiently, low-order spherical harmonics (SH) have long been used [32, 36]. In 3DGS, SH coefficients serve as a finite-dimensional view-dependent radiance head. Our contribution is not to rederive plenoptic bandwidth or SH capacity from scratch, but to reinterpret this frequency transport as a geometric-identifiability condition. We study how a finite SH head can prevent or permit a wrong proxy surface to explain parallax-induced color variation.

Shape–radiance ambiguity in neural fields.

Neural radiance-field methods also expose ambiguities between geometry and view-dependent appearance [28, 47, 38]. Related analyses have observed that color estimation and geometry can be coupled in ways that obscure shape recovery [12]. Our analysis gives a complementary parallax-frequency explanation: bounded angular capacity creates a regime where the true surface is easier to fit than a misaligned proxy, whereas excessive capacity can remove that preference.

3 Background and Motivation

To formally analyze the relationship between angular capacity and geometric correctness, we must first establish how 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) couples geometry with appearance, and how we can mathematically abstract this coupling to expose its core vulnerabilities.

3.1 3DGS, View-Dependence, and Angular Capacity

In 3DGS [20], a scene is not represented by continuous meshes or implicit neural fields, but by an unstructured collection of 3D Gaussian primitives. Each primitive is defined by explicit geometric parameters—a 3D center, a covariance matrix dictating its scale and rotation, and an opacity value. To render a novel view, these primitives are splatted onto the image plane and alpha-composited along camera rays.

Crucially, real-world surfaces exhibit view-dependent appearance, such as specular highlights that shift as the observer moves. To model this, 3DGS does not assign a single static RGB value to a Gaussian. Instead, the emitted color of each primitive is a function of the viewing direction v^∈𝕊2\hat{v}\in\mathbb{S}^{2}. This view-dependence is parameterized using Spherical Harmonics (SH). For each color channel, a Gaussian stores a set of coefficients {cℓ​m}\{c_{\ell m}\}, and the color is evaluated as a linear combination of basis functions:

color​(v^)=∑ℓ=0L∑m=−ℓℓcℓ​m​Yℓ​m​(v^).\text{color}(\hat{v})\ =\ \sum_{\ell=0}^{L}\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}c_{\ell m}Y_{\ell m}(\hat{v}).

Here, Yℓ​mY_{\ell m} denotes the real Spherical Harmonic basis function of degree ℓ\ell and order mm. Conceptually, these basis functions serve as the angular equivalent of a Fourier series on the sphere. The degree ℓ\ell dictates the spatial frequency of the signal: ℓ=0\ell=0 represents a purely diffuse, view-independent color, while higher values of ℓ\ell allow the function to represent sharper, more rapid changes in color as the camera angle shifts.

By truncating this summation at a maximum degree LL, the architecture enforces a strict low-pass filter on the primitive’s angular capacity. This truncation defines a specific function space, which we denote as:

𝒱L:=span{Yℓ​m: 0≤ℓ≤L,−ℓ≤m≤ℓ}.\mathcal{V}_{L}:=\mathrm{span}\{Y_{\ell m}:\ 0\leq\ell\leq L,\ -\ell\leq m\leq\ell\}.

Here, we only allow SH terms up to degree ℓ≤L\ell\leq L. Consequently, the view-dependent color function of each Gaussian is strictly restricted to a finite-dimensional subspace. A larger LL simply expands this space, allowing the model to represent more complex angular dependencies.

3.2 Isolating the Phenomenon: The First-Hit Abstraction

Standard 3DGS rendering relies on volumetric alpha-blending, where the final pixel color is accumulated from multiple semi-transparent Gaussians along a ray. While necessary for gradient flow during early optimization, volumetric compositing obscures the mathematical limits of geometric identifiability by entangling visibility, occlusion, and depth-ordering.

However, the specific failure mode we aim to explain—where a grossly misaligned “billboard” surface fits the training images by painting fake, view-dependent textures—is fundamentally a local, surface-level deception. It occurs because the optimizer places dense, opaque geometry in the wrong physical location, and relies on the SH coefficients of that specific geometry to perfectly mimic the background rays passing through it.

To rigorously study this geometry-appearance tradeoff, we simplify the rendering process to a first-hit abstraction. We assume the optimized geometry forms an opaque surface, meaning the color of any ray is entirely determined by the appearance function of the very first point it intersects. To ground our first-hit abstraction in empirical reality, we conducted a pilot experiment profiling the actual per-ray alpha-compositing weights of a trained 3DGS model. This pilot study reveals an extreme depth-wise concentration: for 92.6% of foreground rays, the front-most 3 contributing Gaussians systematically capture over 90.2% of compositing mass. This statistic should not be interpreted as proving that 3DGS rendering is generally first-hit or opaque. Rather, it provides empirical motivation that, in the mostly opaque scenes used in our controlled experiments, the learned compositing weights are often highly concentrated near the front-most contributors. The first-hit model is therefore best understood as an analytically tractable abstraction of one important regime, not as a faithful model of all 3DGS behavior. For this pilot, we sort contributing Gaussians by depth along each sampled foreground ray and measure the cumulative alpha-compositing mass of the first three contributors.

This abstraction is analytically highly self-consistent because it preserves the exact structural mechanism that enables billboards. It cleanly isolates the core interaction into two distinct roles:

  • •

    Geometry: Which 3D point does the model claim the ray hits first?

  • •

    Appearance: What color must the angular function 𝒱L\mathcal{V}_{L} emit at that specific point to satisfy the training data?

4 Setup and the Geometry-Fixed Projection Principle

To formally evaluate whether the optimization landscape prefers the true geometry over a misaligned one, we abstract the 3DGS rendering process into a minimal first-hit model. This isolates the core geometry-appearance interaction without the confounding effects of volumetric alpha-blending.

4.1 Minimal First-Hit Model and Competing Error Curves

We parameterize a camera ray by its origin y∈ℝ3y\in\mathbb{R}^{3} and viewing direction v^∈𝕊2\hat{v}\in\mathbb{S}^{2}. Let S,U⊂ℝ3S,U\subset\mathbb{R}^{3} denote the true scene geometry and a candidate (potentially misaligned) surface, with respective first-hit points xS​(y,v^)x_{S}(y,\hat{v}) and xU​(y,v^)x_{U}(y,\hat{v}). The ground-truth pixel observation is driven by the true physical appearance C⁡(x,v^)C(x,\hat{v}) defined on the true surface manifold SS, yielding I∗​(y,v^):=C⁡(xS​(y,v^),v^)I^{*}(y,\hat{v}):=C(x_{S}(y,\hat{v}),\hat{v}). If our model commits to the candidate geometry UU, it must assign an appearance function g⁡(x,v^)g(x,\hat{v}) strictly constrained by the angular capacity LL (i.e., g⁡(x,⋅)∈𝒱Lg(x,\cdot)\in\mathcal{V}_{L}). The model’s prediction is thus IU,g​(y,v^):=g⁡(xU​(y,v^),v^)I_{U,g}(y,\hat{v}):=g(x_{U}(y,\hat{v}),\hat{v}).

Let (Y,V^)∼ℙ(Y,\hat{V})\sim\mathbb{P} be a random training ray sampled from the distribution, and define XU:=xU​(Y,V^)X_{U}:=x_{U}(Y,\hat{V}). We call this expected image-space MSE over the ray distribution the population loss: 𝒥⁡(U,g):=𝔼(Y,V^)∼ℙ​[|IU,g​(Y,V^)−I∗​(Y,V^)|2]\mathcal{J}(U,g):=\mathbb{E}_{(Y,\hat{V})\sim\mathbb{P}}[\,|I_{U,g}(Y,\hat{V})-I^{*}(Y,\hat{V})|^{2}\,]. To determine geometric identifiability, we abstract away specific optimizer dynamics and directly evaluate the best-achievable error for both the true and candidate surfaces under the same angular capacity LL:

A⁡(L)\displaystyle A(L) :=infg:g⁡(x,⋅)∈𝒱L𝒥(S,g),\displaystyle:=\inf_{g:\ g(x,\cdot)\in\mathcal{V}_{L}}\ \mathcal{J}(S,g), (1)
BU​(L)\displaystyle B_{U}(L) :=infg:g⁡(x,⋅)∈𝒱L𝒥(U,g).\displaystyle:=\inf_{g:\ g(x,\cdot)\in\mathcal{V}_{L}}\ \mathcal{J}(U,g). (2)

In plain terms, A⁡(L)A(L) measures how well degree LL fits the real appearance given perfect geometry, while BU​(L)B_{U}(L) measures how well degree LL can fake the appearance to compensate for wrong geometry. The entire identifiability narrative reduces to identifying a mathematical regime where A​(L)≪BU​(L)A(L)\ll B_{U}(L).

4.2 Geometry-Fixed Optimality as Pointwise Projection

To evaluate A⁡(L)A(L) and BU​(L)B_{U}(L) without explicitly solving the global optimization, we must first identify the mathematically optimal appearance function for a fixed geometry. Conditioned on hitting a specific physical point x∈Ux\in U, we define the through-seen target FU​(x,⋅)F_{U}(x,\cdot) as the geometry-induced angular target: the colors a candidate point must emit across views to reproduce the true scene. Formally, it is the conditional expectation of the ground-truth image color over the camera origins YY, given the specific hit point and direction V^\hat{V}:

FU(x,⋅):=𝔼[I∗(Y,V^)∣XU=x,V^]F_{U}(x,\cdot):=\mathbb{E}\big[\,I^{*}(Y,\hat{V})\mid X_{U}=x,\hat{V}\,\big] (3)

which yields FU​(x,v^)F_{U}(x,\hat{v}) when evaluated at a specific direction v^\hat{v}. This defines the exact regression function in the angular domain that the training data demands at that location.

Framing the target this way reduces (in our abstraction) the daunting global optimization to independent, local geometric projections.

Proposition 1 (Pointwise projection)

For a fixed surface UU and SH degree LL, the global minimizer of 𝒥⁡(U,g)\mathcal{J}(U,g) is given pointwise by g∗​(x,⋅)=Π𝒱L(x)​(FU​(x,⋅))g^{*}(x,\cdot)=\Pi^{(x)}_{\mathcal{V}_{L}}(F_{U}(x,\cdot)), where Π𝒱L(x)\Pi^{(x)}_{\mathcal{V}_{L}} is the orthogonal projection onto 𝒱L\mathcal{V}_{L} under the L2L^{2} inner product weighted by the conditional viewing distribution at xx. Consequently, the optimal loss is exactly the expected projection distance:

BU​(L)=𝔼x∼μU​[dist(FU​(x,⋅),𝒱L)2].B_{U}(L)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mu_{U}}\big[\,\dist(F_{U}(x,\cdot),\mathcal{V}_{L})^{2}\,\big].

Because the appearance parameters at point xx only affect rays hitting xx, the global integral cleanly decouples into independent least-squares approximations (a rigorous measure-theoretic proof via disintegration is provided in the supplementary material). This principle is crucial: it transforms the geometric identifiability problem into a pure signal-processing question. We now only need to quantify how well the induced target FU​(x,⋅)F_{U}(x,\cdot) can be approximated by the available angular space VLV_{L}. That is, we measure the weighted projection error dist⁡(FU​(x,⋅),VL)\mathrm{dist}(F_{U}(x,\cdot),V_{L}), which precisely corresponds to the residual energy of FUF_{U} in the high-frequency SH degrees ℓ>L\ell>L.

5 The True Surface: Why Smooth Residuals Yield Rapid Decay

To evaluate the best-achievable loss A⁡(L)A(L) on the correct geometry, we must formalize the physical appearance of the true scene. We adopt a decomposition where the ground-truth appearance C⁡(x,v^)C(x,\hat{v}) consists of a view-independent diffuse texture T⁡(x)T(x) and a view-dependent specular residual R⁡(x,v^)R(x,\hat{v}).

Assumption 1 (Diffuse + Sobolev-smooth residual)

The ground-truth appearance on SS decomposes as C=T+RC=T+R. Moreover, there exist strue>0s_{\mathrm{true}}>0 and Mtrue<∞M_{\mathrm{true}}<\infty such that for almost every x∈Sx\in S, the view-dependent residual is mathematically smooth:

‖R⁡(x,⋅)‖Hstrue​(𝕊2)≤Mtrue.\left\lVert R(x,\cdot)\right\rVert_{H^{s_{\mathrm{true}}}(\mathbb{S}^{2})}\leq M_{\mathrm{true}}.

This assumption mathematically enforces that while view-dependent effects like specular highlights exist, they are not arbitrarily sharp or infinitely spiky in direction. The Sobolev norm Hs​(𝕊2)H^{s}(\mathbb{S}^{2}) controls the angular high-frequency energy, meaning a larger ss ensures a stronger decay of SH coefficients. This realistically models most non-mirror materials and is precisely what makes the true surface straightforward to fit.

When the model geometry is perfectly correct, the through-seen target aligns flawlessly with the physical appearance: FS​(x,v^)=T⁡(x)+R⁡(x,v^)F_{S}(x,\hat{v})=T(x)+R(x,\hat{v}). Because the diffuse term T⁡(x)T(x) does not change with the viewing direction v^\hat{v}, it resides entirely within the SH degree-0 subspace (𝒱0⊂𝒱L\mathcal{V}_{0}\subset\mathcal{V}_{L}).

Consequently, the spatial complexity of the true texture—no matter how high-frequency or intricate—consumes absolutely zero angular capacity. The approximation difficulty stems exclusively from the residual RR:

dist(FS​(x,⋅),𝒱L)=dist(R⁡(x,⋅),𝒱L).\dist\big(F_{S}(x,\cdot),\mathcal{V}_{L}\big)=\dist\big(R(x,\cdot),\mathcal{V}_{L}\big).

Because RR is assumed to be Sobolev-smooth, its projection error onto a bandlimited SH subspace naturally decays. We formalize this using standard spectral approximation on the sphere (full derivation provided in the supplementary material):

Lemma 1 (Sobolev smoothness implies fast SH truncation)

Let P≤LP_{\leq L} be the L2​(𝕊2)L^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{2}) orthogonal projection onto 𝒱L\mathcal{V}_{L}. If f∈Hs​(𝕊2)f\in H^{s}(\mathbb{S}^{2}), then its truncation error is bounded by:

‖f−P≤L​f‖L2​(𝕊2)2≤(1+L⁡(L+1))−s​‖f‖Hs​(𝕊2)2.\left\lVert f-P_{\leq L}f\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{2})}^{2}\ \leq\ \big(1+L(L+1)\big)^{-s}\ \left\lVert f\right\rVert_{H^{s}(\mathbb{S}^{2})}^{2}.

(For simplicity, we state the truncation bound under the uniform sphere measure; extending this to pointwise weighted norms requires mild density bounds on νU(⋅∣x)\nu_{U}(\cdot\mid x), as detailed in the supplementary material).

This rate comes from the Laplace–Beltrami eigenvalues ℓ⁡(ℓ+1)\ell(\ell+1), which define the Sobolev weights (1+ℓ⁡(ℓ+1))s(1+\ell(\ell+1))^{s}. Truncating the expansion at the maximum degree LL then yields the specific factor (1+L⁡(L+1))−s(1+L(L+1))^{-s} observed in the error bound. Bounding the Sobolev norm directly suppresses the energy in the tail ℓ>L\ell>L. By applying this lemma to our residual, we immediately establish the upper bound for the true surface.

Proposition 2 (True-surface upper bound)

Under Assumption 1, the best achievable loss on the true surface satisfies:

A⁡(L)≤(1+L⁡(L+1))−strue​Mtrue2,A(L)\ \leq\ \big(1+L(L+1)\big)^{-s_{\mathrm{true}}}\,M_{\mathrm{true}}^{2},

up to a multiplicative constant depending only on view-direction sampling.

The proof follows directly from our pointwise projection principle (Proposition 1). Since T⁡(x)T(x) projects with zero error, the squared distance

dist(FS​(x,⋅),𝒱L)2\dist(F_{S}(x,\cdot),\mathcal{V}_{L})^{2}

is simply the truncation error of R⁡(x,⋅)R(x,\cdot). Applying Lemma 1 and averaging over the surface points yields the bound.

This result establishes a critical baseline: A⁡(L)A(L) drops rapidly with LL. A moderate SH degree is more than sufficient to make the true surface an attractive minimum for the optimizer. If this were the whole story, one might assume that simply increasing LL is harmless. However, as we demonstrate next, a misaligned geometry interacts with diffuse texture in a fundamentally different way, forcefully converting spatial details into high-frequency angular signals.

6 The Misaligned Surface: Parallax Forges High Angular Frequencies

Having established that the true surface inherently requires very little angular capacity, we now turn to what happens when the model proposes a geometrically misaligned candidate. We aim to show that wrong geometry is penalized heavily because it forces spatial complexity to masquerade as angular complexity.

6.1 Formalizing the Billboard Scenario

To analyze the “opaque billboard” failure mode, where incorrect geometry achieves optimal appearance, we establish three minimal conditions.

Assumption 2 (Visible texture mode)

There exists a visible surface patch and a local tangential coordinate uu such that the true diffuse texture T⁡(u)T(u) contains a sinusoidal component a​sin⁡(k​u)a\sin(ku) with amplitude a>0a>0 and spatial frequency k>0k>0.

Assumption 3 (Visible misalignment magnitude)

On a visible set of rays, the candidate surface UU is misaligned from the true surface SS by a non-negligible depth gap Δ​z>0\Delta z>0.

Assumption 4 (Residual cannot erase texture)

The true specular residual RR is not strong enough to adversarially cancel the spatial texture: there exists 0≤ρ<10\leq\rho<1 such that |R⁡(x,v^)|≤ρ​a|R(x,\hat{v})|\leq\rho a.

These assumptions collectively define the basic requirements for geometry to be visually identifiable from RGB alone. If the scene lacks texture entirely (Assumption 2 fails) or the residual completely washes out the diffuse color (Assumption 4 fails), the optimization lacks the necessary signal to distinguish depth. If the depth gap is negligible (Assumption 3 fails), the candidate surface effectively behaves like the true surface.

Material-model limitation.

Assumption 4 excludes view-dependent effects that can cancel or dominate diffuse texture, including mirrors, inter-reflections, transparency, exposure/white-balance changes, and nonlinear tone mapping. Then the residual may itself carry high angular frequency, breaking our spatial-texture/angular-residual separation.

6.2 The Frequency Transport Law via Parallax

To see exactly how angular complexity is generated by geometric error, consider a standard 2D cross-section for parallax analysis. Place the camera at the origin, let the true surface be the line z=zgtz=z_{\mathrm{gt}}, and let the candidate surface be a billboard at z=zfakez=z_{\mathrm{fake}}, yielding a depth gap Δ​z:=zgt−zfake>0\Delta z:=z_{\mathrm{gt}}-z_{\mathrm{fake}}>0. We parameterize the camera rays by a sweeping angle α\alpha. Equivalently, assume a moving camera observing a fixed physical point x0x_{0} on the fake surface from different view angles α\alpha. See Fig. 2 for a visual illustration of both the geometric transport and the induced view-to-color mapping.

A direct geometric computation (supplementary material) reveals that if a ray first hits the wrong surface at lateral coordinate x0x_{0}, the physical hit point on the true background surface moves according to:

xhit​(α)=x0+Δ​z​tan⁡α.x_{\mathrm{hit}}(\alpha)\ =\ x_{0}+\Delta z\,\tan\alpha. (4)

Consequently, when the model evaluates the loss on the wrong surface, its through-seen target function FUF_{U} must pull the color from the background texture T​(xhit​(α))T(x_{\mathrm{hit}}(\alpha))(the residual term RR is handled via Assumption 4 and the supplementary material). Using our assumed texture component and approximating tan⁡α≈α\tan\alpha\approx\alpha for moderate viewing angles, the target signal on the wrong surface becomes:

a​sin⁡(k⁡(x0+Δ​z​α))=a​sin⁡(k​x0+(k​Δ​z)​α).a\sin\!\big(k(x_{0}+\Delta z\alpha)\big)\ =\ a\sin\!\big(kx_{0}+(k\Delta z)\alpha\big).

This reveals a profound physical transformation: the spatial frequency kk has been forcefully multiplied by the depth error Δ​z\Delta z to generate a new angular frequency:

ωfake≈k​Δ​z.\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}\ \approx\ k\Delta z. (5)

This scale law dictates the appearance burden placed on wrong geometry: finer textures or larger depth errors demand increasingly rapid angular color shifts.

6.3 The Immutable Lower Bound for Wrong Geometry

This induced angular frequency creates a mathematical bottleneck. As established earlier, any SH basis of degree LL acts as a low-pass filter along viewing arcs.

Lemma 2 (Bandlimit along great circles)

If h∈𝒱Lh\in\mathcal{V}_{L}, restricting hh to any great circle yields a 1D trigonometric polynomial with maximum frequency LL.

When the induced frequency exceeds the model’s capacity (L<ωfakeL<\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}), the model is mathematically incapable of fitting the signal. For analytical clarity, we use a global Fourier bound rather than relying only on local linearization. This is governed by a fundamental property of Fourier approximation (proven in the supplementary material):

Lemma 3 (High frequency cannot be fit by low frequency)

Suppose the frequency ω\omega is an integer. Consider f⁡(ϕ)=a​sin⁡(ω​ϕ)f(\phi)=a\sin(\omega\phi) on [0,2​π][0,2\pi]. The best L2L^{2} approximation of ff by any trigonometric polynomial of degree L<ωL<\omega leaves an unavoidable residual error strictly bounded away from zero.

Because the specular residual cannot completely erase the texture (Assumption 4), we can invoke the triangle inequality on the function spaces to guarantee that the projection error of the combined signal remains large. This culminates in our strict lower bound for misaligned geometry.

Here a≍ba\asymp b denotes equality up to constants independent of LL.

Proposition 3 (Misaligned-surface lower bound)

Under Assumption 2, Assumption 3, and Assumption 4, there exist ωfake≍k​Δ​z\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}\asymp k\Delta z and a constant c0>0c_{0}>0 such that for all angular capacities L<ωfakeL<\omega_{\mathrm{fake}},

BU​(L)≥c0.B_{U}(L)\ \geq\ c_{0}.

The proof mechanically links our findings: the through-seen function on a misaligned patch contains an angular sinusoid of frequency ωfake≈k​Δ​z\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}\approx k\Delta z. By Lemma 2, the 𝒱L\mathcal{V}_{L} appearance function cannot exceed frequency LL along this viewing circle. Thus, whenever L<ωfakeL<\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}, Lemma 3 ensures a massive, unoptimizable constant error on this patch, which lower-bounds the global integral BU​(L)B_{U}(L). We now possess the two essential halves of the identifiability story: the true surface benefits from a fast-decaying upper bound A⁡(L)A(L), while the wrong surface suffers from a stubborn lower bound BU​(L)B_{U}(L). By synthesizing these bounds, we can explicitly characterize the intermediate capacity window that successfully recovers accurate 3D geometry.

7 Putting It Together: The Identifiability Window

We are finally positioned to synthesize the two halves of our analysis. By juxtaposing the rapid decay of the true surface’s approximation error with the stubborn constant lower bound of the misaligned surface, the theoretical mechanism behind 3DGS geometric identifiability emerges clearly (see the supplementary material for a numeric example).

Theorem 7.1 (Intermediate-LL identifiability window)

Under Assumption 2, Assumption 3, and Assumption 4, there exist constants c0>0c_{0}>0 and ωfake≍k​Δ​z\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}\asymp k\Delta z such that: (i) for all L≥0L\geq 0, A⁡(L)≤(1+L⁡(L+1))−strue​Mtrue2A(L)\leq(1+L(L+1))^{-s_{\mathrm{true}}}M_{\mathrm{true}}^{2} (up to view-sampling constants); and (ii) for all L<ωfakeL<\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}, BU​(L)≥c0B_{U}(L)\geq c_{0}. Therefore, any LL satisfying (1+L⁡(L+1))−strue​Mtrue2<c0(1+L(L+1))^{-s_{\mathrm{true}}}M_{\mathrm{true}}^{2}<c_{0} and L<ωfakeL<\omega_{\mathrm{fake}} guarantees a strict separation A​(L)<BU​(L)A(L)<B_{U}(L): the true surface is strictly easier to fit than the misaligned surface UU under angular capacity LL.

This theorem rigorously partitions the angular capacity of 3DGS into three distinct regimes. When LL is too small, the model cannot fit the true specular residual RR, yielding high error for all candidate geometries. In the intermediate regime, A⁡(L)A(L) collapses as the true smooth residual is approximated, yet BU​(L)B_{U}(L) remains trapped by the L<ωfakeL<\omega_{\mathrm{fake}} barrier, creating the optimal geometry-identifiable window. However, once L≳ωfakeL\gtrsim\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}, this lower-bound mechanism vanishes, clarifying the opaque billboard paradox introduced earlier. As proven in the supplementary material, the SH basis becomes expressive enough to memorize the parallax-induced false texture, allowing a misaligned surface to achieve exactly zero population loss. In this over-parameterized regime, the optimizer is mathematically permitted to “cheat”: it can erect an arbitrary, vision-blocking sheet in empty space and task the high-degree Spherical Harmonics with projecting the missing background spatial frequencies as rapid, view-dependent color shifts.

8 Experiment

Datasets.

We construct a synthetic dataset of 100 shapes (25 base geometries ×\times 4 variants) to systematically trigger and evaluate the failure modes predicted in Sec. 5–7. Real-world benchmarks typically feature rich, high-frequency spatial textures (large kk), which naturally drive the required angular frequency ωfake≈k​Δ​z\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}\approx k\Delta z beyond typical SH capacities. By using synthetic shapes with tunable complexity under controlled lighting, we can deliberately evaluate the vulnerability to billboard collapse.

We additionally evaluate the same diagnostic on ten real-scene datasets with available geometry where 3DGS can be trained (Section 8.2). These real-world experiments probe whether opaque billboard failures arise in practice when using high SH degrees under standard multi-view capture protocols. Under our labeling criterion, we find no opaque-billboard cases: across these datasets the learned Gaussians remain surface-consistent even at large angular capacity, in line with the “safe” regime predicted by our theory.

We train 3DGS with default hyperparameters and vary only the SH degree L. Geometry is evaluated by normalized symmetric Chamfer distance (nCD) between Gaussian centers and GT surfaces; appearance by PSNR. We define “opaque billboard” as runs with near-best PSNR but severely degraded nCD; full protocol and thresholds and the definitions of billboard failure, billboard onset, outlier point removal are in the supplementary material.

8.1 Opaque billboard failure at large angular capacity

Section 7 predicts that when the angular capacity LL exceeds the induced frequency threshold ωfake\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}, opaque billboard solutions can perfectly minimize the training objective. Our synthetic experiments strongly support this prediction: when LL is made sufficiently large, we frequently observe opaque billboard failures, where 3DGS no longer reconstructs the true surface but still produces high-quality renderings. The observed dense layers are consistent with our first-hit regime, but do not imply all 3DGS rendering behaves this way. As shown in Fig. 3, we observe three consistent patterns. (a) As the SH degree increases, approximately  89% of shapes generally increase in nCD between the Gaussian centers and the ground-truth surface, while the average PSNR slightly increases. For these shapes, the high-SH runs are labeled as either billboard-onset or opaque billboard under our criterion: nCD grows to several times nCDbest\text{nCD}_{\text{best}} even though PSNR stays within 22 dB of PSNRbest\text{PSNR}_{\text{best}}. This indicates that as the angular capacity grows, the Gaussians gain enough representational power that they no longer need to stay on the surface to provide good renderings. (b) Among the shapes that drift away from the surface, we see two dominant behaviors, which correspond to the two medians in Fig. 3. For roughly  42% of cases, nCD grows almost linearly with SH degree (the dashed green “linear” median), leading to billboard-onset or opaque-billboard labels only at the highest SH degrees. For roughly  53% of cases, nCD remains small up to a moderate SH degree and then undergoes a sharp increase once SH enters the range 6–12 (the solid blue “burst” median). In these “burst” cases the high-SH runs are almost always labeled as opaque billboard: beyond a certain angular capacity, the Gaussians can fit the appearance almost entirely by adjusting their SH coefficients without moving in space. (c) Finally, Fig. 3 also shows that, for a subset of objects, no opaque-billboard regime appears: all runs for these shapes remain surface-consistent under our labeling criterion. Even at high SH degrees, nCD stays within 2×nCDbest2\times\text{nCD}_{\text{best}} and the learned Gaussians stay close to the ground-truth surface. These cases match the “safe” identifiability window predicted by our theory, where higher spatial complexity (large kk) pushes the required angular frequency beyond our tested capacities, which effectively mitigates this failure mode in practical settings.

8.2 Real-scene experiments

Do opaque billboard failures occur on real objects under standard capture protocols? To answer this question, we train 3DGS with varying SH degrees on ten real-scene datasets with ground-truth geometry where 3DGS can be applied: DTU [1], MobileBrick [23], YCB-Video [44], T-LESS [17], ScanNet [8], ScanNet++ [46], Matterport3D [6], HM3D [31], Tanks & Temples [21], and ETH3D [34] (Table 1). For each dataset we apply the same billboard labeling criterion as in the synthetic experiments.

Across all objects and SH degrees, we do not observe any run that satisfies the opaque-billboard condition: no run simultaneously has PSNR within 22 dB of the per-object PSNRbest\text{PSNR}_{\text{best}} and nCD at least 5×5\times nCDbest\text{nCD}_{\text{best}}. Under this PSNR band, nCD remains tightly concentrated: as summarized in Table 1, for every dataset the nCD at SH=24\mathrm{SH}=24 differs from that at SH=3\mathrm{SH}=3 by at most a factor of about 1.2×1.2\times. In other words, increasing angular capacity in these real-scene settings does not lead to the large geometric drifts that characterize opaque billboard failures.

Thus, within standard multi-view capture protocols on these diverse real-world benchmarks, the learned Gaussians remain surface-consistent according to our criterion. This empirical finding is consistent with our theoretical frequency scale law: typical real-scene setups are characterized by rich spatial textures (very large kk). This naturally drives the parallax-induced frequency ωfake≈k​Δ​z\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}\approx k\Delta z so high that even large capacities like SH=24\mathrm{SH}=24 cannot bridge the gap (L≪ωfakeL\ll\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}). Consequently, the model remains within the geometry-identifiable window in our tested settings, favoring surface-consistent solutions over billboard collapse.

9 Conclusion & Discussion

Increasing angular capacity is a double-edged sword: it helps fit specularities, but can let misaligned geometry explain away parallax-induced texture. This yields an intermediate-LL identifiability window and supports capacity scheduling, e.g., starting with low LL. Our guarantees apply to mostly opaque scenes with smooth view-dependent residuals; mirror-like, transparent, or strongly camera-processed scenes may require geometry or material priors.

Effect of geometric regularization.

Our analysis studies the image reconstruction objective with bounded angular radiance capacity. Geometry-aware variants such as surface-aligned Gaussian methods, 2D Gaussian formulations, SDF-coupled methods, or normal/depth regularization modify this problem by either restricting the admissible geometry class or adding explicit penalties against off-surface solutions. Such priors can shrink or remove the billboard-favorable regime predicted by our theorem. Thus, our results should not be read as a claim that geometry-aware methods fail in the same way; rather, they explain why such geometric priors are valuable when angular appearance capacity is large.

Appendix 0.A Proof of the Pointwise Projection Proposition

Here we prove the pointwise projection proposition in the main paper.

0.A.1 Measurable setup and induced hit-point measures

xU:ℛ→U,(y,v^)↦xU​(y,v^)x_{U}:\ \mathcal{R}\to U,\qquad(y,\hat{v})\mapsto x_{U}(y,\hat{v})

is measurable on the subset of rays for which the first hit exists and is unique.11 1 If non-uniqueness occurs on a ℙ\mathbb{P}-null set (e.g., tangential rays), it can be resolved by any measurable tie-breaking rule without affecting the population loss.

XU:=xU​(Y,V^)∈U,X_{U}:=x_{U}(Y,\hat{V})\in U,

νU:=(XU,V^)#​ℙ,\nu_{U}\ :=\ (X_{U},\hat{V})_{\#}\mathbb{P},

μU:=(πU)#​νU,πU​(x,v^)=x.\mu_{U}:=(\pi_{U})_{\#}\nu_{U},\qquad\pi_{U}(x,\hat{v})=x.

By the disintegration theorem (existence of regular conditional probabilities on standard Borel spaces), there exists a μU\mu_{U}-a.e. defined family of conditional probability measures {νU(⋅∣x)}x∈U\{\nu_{U}(\cdot\mid x)\}_{x\in U} on 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2} such that for every bounded measurable ψ\psi,

∫U×𝕊2ψ⁡(x,v^)​d​νU​(x,v^)=∫U(∫𝕊2ψ⁡(x,v^)​d​νU​(v^∣x))​d​μU​(x).\int_{U\times\mathbb{S}^{2}}\psi(x,\hat{v})\,d\nu_{U}(x,\hat{v})=\int_{U}\left(\int_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}\psi(x,\hat{v})\,d\nu_{U}(\hat{v}\mid x)\right)\,d\mu_{U}(x). (6)

0.A.2 Replacing raw pixels by the through-seen target via conditional expectation

Recall the ground-truth pixel random variable along a sampled ray:

Z:=I∗​(Y,V^)∈ℝ(or ​ℝ3​ channel-wise).Z:=I^{*}(Y,\hat{V})\in\mathbb{R}\quad(\text{or }\mathbb{R}^{3}\text{ channel-wise}).

For fixed geometry UU, define the through-seen ground-truth target as the regular conditional expectation

FU(x,v^):=𝔼[Z|XU=x,V^=v^],F_{U}(x,\hat{v})\ :=\ \mathbb{E}\!\left[\,Z\ \middle|\ X_{U}=x,\ \hat{V}=\hat{v}\,\right], (7)

interpreted as any νU\nu_{U}-a.e. version of the conditional expectation 𝔼⁡[Z|σ⁡(XU,V^)]\mathbb{E}[Z\,|\,\sigma(X_{U},\hat{V})] evaluated at (x,v^)(x,\hat{v}).

For any admissible appearance function gg on UU (with g⁡(x,⋅)∈𝒱Lg(x,\cdot)\in\mathcal{V}_{L} for all xx), the population loss is

𝒥⁡(U,g)=𝔼⁡[|g⁡(XU,V^)−Z|2].\mathcal{J}(U,g)=\mathbb{E}\Big[\big|g(X_{U},\hat{V})-Z\big|^{2}\Big].

Applying the tower property conditional on (XU,V^)(X_{U},\hat{V}) gives

𝒥⁡(U,g)\displaystyle\mathcal{J}(U,g) =𝔼[𝔼[|g(XU,V^)−Z|2|XU,V^]]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Big[\,\mathbb{E}\big[\big|g(X_{U},\hat{V})-Z\big|^{2}\ \big|\ X_{U},\hat{V}\big]\,\Big] (8)
=𝔼⁡[|g⁡(XU,V^)−FU​(XU,V^)|2+Var⁡(Z∣XU,V^)].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Big[\ \big|g(X_{U},\hat{V})-F_{U}(X_{U},\hat{V})\big|^{2}\ +\ \Var\!\big(Z\mid X_{U},\hat{V}\big)\ \Big]. (9)

The conditional variance term is independent of gg. Hence minimizing 𝒥⁡(U,g)\mathcal{J}(U,g) over admissible gg is equivalent to minimizing

𝔼⁡[|g⁡(XU,V^)−FU​(XU,V^)|2]=∫U×𝕊2|g⁡(x,v^)−FU​(x,v^)|2​d​νU​(x,v^).\mathbb{E}\Big[\big|g(X_{U},\hat{V})-F_{U}(X_{U},\hat{V})\big|^{2}\Big]=\int_{U\times\mathbb{S}^{2}}\big|g(x,\hat{v})-F_{U}(x,\hat{v})\big|^{2}\,d\nu_{U}(x,\hat{v}). (10)

0.A.3 Pointwise decoupling of the minimization and the weighted projection

Using the disintegration (6) in (10), we rewrite:

𝒥(U,g)≡∫U[∫𝕊2|g⁡(x,v^)−FU​(x,v^)|2​d​νU​(v^∣x)]⏟=:Φx​(g⁡(x,⋅))dμU(x)+const(U).\mathcal{J}(U,g)\equiv\int_{U}\underbrace{\left[\int_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}\big|g(x,\hat{v})-F_{U}(x,\hat{v})\big|^{2}\,d\nu_{U}(\hat{v}\mid x)\right]}_{=:~\Phi_{x}(g(x,\cdot))}\,d\mu_{U}(x)\quad+\ \text{const}(U). (11)

Crucially, for fixed geometry UU, the function g⁡(x,⋅)g(x,\cdot) appears only inside the term Φx​(⋅)\Phi_{x}(\,\cdot\,) indexed by the same point xx. Therefore, the global minimization decouples:

infg:g⁡(x,⋅)∈𝒱L𝒥(U,g)⟺for μU-a.e. x, solve minh∈𝒱LΦx(h).\inf_{g:\ g(x,\cdot)\in\mathcal{V}_{L}}\ \mathcal{J}(U,g)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{for $\mu_{U}$-a.e.\ $x$, solve }\ \min_{h\in\mathcal{V}_{L}}\ \Phi_{x}(h). (12)

For each fixed xx, define the weighted Hilbert space L2(𝕊2,νU(⋅∣x))L^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{2},\nu_{U}(\cdot\mid x)) with inner product

⟨f,h⟩x:=∫𝕊2f⁡(v^)​h​(v^)​d​νU​(v^∣x),‖f‖x2:=⟨f,f⟩x.\langle f,h\rangle_{x}:=\int_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}f(\hat{v})\,h(\hat{v})\,d\nu_{U}(\hat{v}\mid x),\qquad\|f\|_{x}^{2}:=\langle f,f\rangle_{x}.

Since 𝒱L\mathcal{V}_{L} is finite-dimensional, it is a closed subspace of this Hilbert space, and the standard least-squares theorem implies:

hx∗​(⋅):=arg⁡minh∈𝒱L⁡‖h−FU​(x,⋅)‖x2=Π𝒱L(x)​(FU​(x,⋅)),h_{x}^{*}(\cdot)\ :=\ \arg\min_{h\in\mathcal{V}_{L}}\ \|h-F_{U}(x,\cdot)\|_{x}^{2}\ =\ \Pi^{(x)}_{\mathcal{V}_{L}}\big(F_{U}(x,\cdot)\big), (13)

where Π𝒱L(x)\Pi^{(x)}_{\mathcal{V}_{L}} denotes the orthogonal projection w.r.t. ⟨⋅,⋅⟩x\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{x}.

Define the global minimizer pointwise by g∗​(x,⋅):=hx∗​(⋅)g^{*}(x,\cdot):=h_{x}^{*}(\cdot). Plugging back into (11) yields the minimal achievable loss:

infg:g⁡(x,⋅)∈𝒱L𝒥(U,g)=𝔼x∼μU[dist(FU(x,⋅),𝒱L)2]+const(U),\inf_{g:\ g(x,\cdot)\in\mathcal{V}_{L}}\ \mathcal{J}(U,g)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mu_{U}}\Big[\,\dist\big(F_{U}(x,\cdot),\mathcal{V}_{L}\big)^{2}\,\Big]\quad+\ \text{const}(U), (14)

where the distance is taken in the weighted L2(𝕊2,νU(⋅∣x))L^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{2},\nu_{U}(\cdot\mid x)) norm.

This proves the pointwise projection proposition in the main paper (absorbing the gg-independent variance term into the definition of BU​(L)B_{U}(L), or equivalently by defining FUF_{U} as the conditional expectation target).

0.A.4 Explicit coefficient form (optional, useful for intuition)

Write a basis of 𝒱L\mathcal{V}_{L} as {ψq}q=1Q\{\psi_{q}\}_{q=1}^{Q} where Q=(L+1)2Q=(L+1)^{2} (e.g. ψq=Yℓ​m\psi_{q}=Y_{\ell m}). For fixed xx, represent h⁡(v^)=∑q=1Qaq​(x)​ψq​(v^)h(\hat{v})=\sum_{q=1}^{Q}a_{q}(x)\psi_{q}(\hat{v}). Then (13) is equivalent to the normal equations:

∑q′=1QGq​q′​(x)​aq′​(x)=bq​(x),Gq​q′​(x):=⟨ψq,ψq′⟩x,bq​(x):=⟨FU​(x,⋅),ψq⟩x.\sum_{q^{\prime}=1}^{Q}G_{qq^{\prime}}(x)\,a_{q^{\prime}}(x)=b_{q}(x),\qquad G_{qq^{\prime}}(x):=\langle\psi_{q},\psi_{q^{\prime}}\rangle_{x},\quad b_{q}(x):=\langle F_{U}(x,\cdot),\psi_{q}\rangle_{x}. (15)

If νU(⋅∣x)\nu_{U}(\cdot\mid x) is uniform on 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2}, then G⁡(x)G(x) is the identity for an orthonormal SH basis, and aq​(x)=bq​(x)a_{q}(x)=b_{q}(x) are exactly the SH coefficients up to degree LL.

Appendix 0.B Sobolev Smoothness and Spherical Harmonic Truncation

This appendix provides the detailed derivation underlying the Sobolev truncation lemma in the main paper and explains the origin of the factor 1+ℓ⁡(ℓ+1)1+\ell(\ell+1) from the Laplace–Beltrami spectrum on 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2}.

0.B.1 Spherical harmonics and Laplace–Beltrami eigenvalues

Let d​ωd\omega be the uniform area measure on 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2}. The (complex) spherical harmonics {Yℓ​m}ℓ≥0,−ℓ≤m≤ℓ\{Y_{\ell m}\}_{\ell\geq 0,\ -\ell\leq m\leq\ell} form a complete orthonormal basis of L2​(𝕊2,d​ω)L^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{2},d\omega):

⟨Yℓ​m,Yℓ′​m′⟩L2​(𝕊2)=∫𝕊2Yℓ​m​(v^)​Yℓ′​m′​(v^)¯​𝑑ω​(v^)=δℓ​ℓ′​δm​m′.\langle Y_{\ell m},Y_{\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}}\rangle_{L^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{2})}=\int_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}Y_{\ell m}(\hat{v})\,\overline{Y_{\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}}(\hat{v})}\,d\omega(\hat{v})=\delta_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}\delta_{mm^{\prime}}.

(Real spherical harmonics satisfy the same orthonormality and eigenvalue relations; all arguments below apply verbatim.)

A fundamental identity is that Yℓ​mY_{\ell m} are eigenfunctions of the spherical Laplacian Δ𝕊2\Delta_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}:

Δ𝕊2​Yℓ​m=−ℓ⁡(ℓ+1)​Yℓ​m.\Delta_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}Y_{\ell m}\ =\ -\ell(\ell+1)\,Y_{\ell m}. (16)

0.B.2 Spectral definition of Sobolev norms on the sphere

For f∈L2​(𝕊2)f\in L^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{2}), write its SH expansion

f⁡(v^)=∑ℓ=0∞∑m=−ℓℓfℓ​m​Yℓ​m​(v^),fℓ​m:=⟨f,Yℓ​m⟩L2​(𝕊2).f(\hat{v})=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}f_{\ell m}Y_{\ell m}(\hat{v}),\qquad f_{\ell m}:=\langle f,Y_{\ell m}\rangle_{L^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{2})}.

Define the (spectral) Sobolev norm for s≥0s\geq 0 by

‖f‖Hs​(𝕊2)2:=∑ℓ=0∞∑m=−ℓℓ(1+ℓ⁡(ℓ+1))s​|fℓ​m|2.\|f\|_{H^{s}(\mathbb{S}^{2})}^{2}:=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}\big(1+\ell(\ell+1)\big)^{s}\,|f_{\ell m}|^{2}. (17)

The factor 1+ℓ⁡(ℓ+1)1+\ell(\ell+1) arises because (I−Δ𝕊2)​Yℓ​m=(1+ℓ⁡(ℓ+1))​Yℓ​m(I-\Delta_{\mathbb{S}^{2}})Y_{\ell m}=(1+\ell(\ell+1))Y_{\ell m} by (16). For integer ss, this norm is equivalent (up to constants) to the classical definition involving tangential derivatives on the sphere.

0.B.3 Proof of the Sobolev truncation lemma

Here we prove the Sobolev truncation lemma in the main paper.

Let P≤LP_{\leq L} denote the L2​(𝕊2)L^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{2}) orthogonal projection onto

𝒱L=span{Yℓ​m:0≤ℓ≤L,−ℓ≤m≤ℓ},\mathcal{V}_{L}=\mathrm{span}\{Y_{\ell m}:0\leq\ell\leq L,\ -\ell\leq m\leq\ell\},

i.e.,

(P≤L​f)​(v^)=∑ℓ=0L∑m=−ℓℓfℓ​m​Yℓ​m​(v^).(P_{\leq L}f)(\hat{v})=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}f_{\ell m}Y_{\ell m}(\hat{v}).

By orthonormality, the truncation error energy is exactly the discarded coefficient tail:

‖f−P≤L​f‖L2​(𝕊2)2=∑ℓ=L+1∞∑m=−ℓℓ|fℓ​m|2.\|f-P_{\leq L}f\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{2})}^{2}=\sum_{\ell=L+1}^{\infty}\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}|f_{\ell m}|^{2}. (18)

For every ℓ>L\ell>L, we have (1+ℓ⁡(ℓ+1))s≥(1+L⁡(L+1))s(1+\ell(\ell+1))^{s}\geq(1+L(L+1))^{s}, hence

|fℓ​m|2≤(1+L⁡(L+1))−s​(1+ℓ⁡(ℓ+1))s​|fℓ​m|2.|f_{\ell m}|^{2}\leq(1+L(L+1))^{-s}\,(1+\ell(\ell+1))^{s}\,|f_{\ell m}|^{2}.

Summing over ℓ>L\ell>L and mm and using (18) yields

‖f−P≤L​f‖L2​(𝕊2)2\displaystyle\|f-P_{\leq L}f\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{2})}^{2} ≤(1+L⁡(L+1))−s​∑ℓ=0∞∑m=−ℓℓ(1+ℓ⁡(ℓ+1))s​|fℓ​m|2\displaystyle\leq(1+L(L+1))^{-s}\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}(1+\ell(\ell+1))^{s}|f_{\ell m}|^{2}
=(1+L⁡(L+1))−s​‖f‖Hs​(𝕊2)2,\displaystyle=(1+L(L+1))^{-s}\,\|f\|_{H^{s}(\mathbb{S}^{2})}^{2},

which is exactly the Sobolev truncation lemma in the main paper.

0.B.4 Remark on non-uniform view-direction sampling (why we say “up to constants”)

In the paper, projections at each surface point xx are taken w.r.t. the conditional direction distribution νU(⋅∣x)\nu_{U}(\cdot\mid x), not necessarily the uniform measure d​ωd\omega. If νU(⋅∣x)\nu_{U}(\cdot\mid x) admits a density wx​(v^)w_{x}(\hat{v}) w.r.t. d​ωd\omega satisfying 0<wmin≤wx​(v^)≤wmax<∞0<w_{\min}\leq w_{x}(\hat{v})\leq w_{\max}<\infty uniformly on the region of interest, then the weighted norm ∥f∥L2(νU(⋅∣x))\|f\|_{L^{2}(\nu_{U}(\cdot\mid x))} is equivalent to ‖f‖L2​(d​ω)\|f\|_{L^{2}(d\omega)} with constants wmin,wmaxw_{\min},w_{\max}. Consequently, all truncation bounds transfer to the weighted inner products with only multiplicative constants depending on these density bounds, justifying the “up to view-sampling constants” language in the true-surface upper-bound proposition in the main paper.

Appendix 0.C Parallax Calculus and Frequency Lower Bounds for Misaligned Surfaces

This appendix provides (i) the explicit parallax derivation behind the parallax hit-point relation in the main paper and the induced-frequency relation in the main paper, (ii) a detailed proof of the great-circle bandlimit lemma in the main paper, and (iii) the Fourier approximation lower bound used in the Fourier lower-bound lemma in the main paper and the misaligned-surface lower-bound proposition in the main paper.

0.C.1 Deriving the parallax hit-point relation

Here we derive the parallax hit-point relation in the main paper.

Consider the standard 2D cross-section model (a local linearization of two nearby surface patches): the camera center is at the origin, and we use coordinates (x,z)(x,z) in the viewing plane.

Let the true surface be the line z=zgtz=z_{\mathrm{gt}} and the candidate (misaligned) surface be z=zfakez=z_{\mathrm{fake}}. Define the depth gap

Δ​z:=zgt−zfake.\Delta z:=z_{\mathrm{gt}}-z_{\mathrm{fake}}.

Parameterize rays by an angle α\alpha (relative to the positive zz-axis). A ray from the origin with angle α\alpha has direction proportional to (tan⁡α,1)(\tan\alpha,1), hence can be written as

(x,z)=(t​tan⁡α,t),t>0.(x,z)=(t\tan\alpha,t),\qquad t>0.

This ray intersects z=zfakez=z_{\mathrm{fake}} at t=zfaket=z_{\mathrm{fake}}, with xx-coordinate

xfake​(α)=zfake​tan⁡α.x_{\mathrm{fake}}(\alpha)=z_{\mathrm{fake}}\tan\alpha.

Similarly, it intersects z=zgtz=z_{\mathrm{gt}} at t=zgtt=z_{\mathrm{gt}}, with coordinate

xgt​(α)=zgt​tan⁡α.x_{\mathrm{gt}}(\alpha)=z_{\mathrm{gt}}\tan\alpha.

Now fix a specific point on the fake surface with coordinate x0x_{0}. For the ray that hits this fake point, we have xfake​(α)=x0x_{\mathrm{fake}}(\alpha)=x_{0}, hence

x0=zfake​tan⁡α.x_{0}=z_{\mathrm{fake}}\tan\alpha.

For that same ray, the true intersection point is

xhit​(α)\displaystyle x_{\mathrm{hit}}(\alpha) =xgt​(α)=zgt​tan⁡α=zfake​tan⁡α+(zgt−zfake)​tan⁡α\displaystyle=x_{\mathrm{gt}}(\alpha)=z_{\mathrm{gt}}\tan\alpha=z_{\mathrm{fake}}\tan\alpha+(z_{\mathrm{gt}}-z_{\mathrm{fake}})\tan\alpha (19)
=x0+Δ​z​tan⁡α,\displaystyle=x_{0}+\Delta z\,\tan\alpha, (20)

which is the parallax hit-point relation in the main paper.

0.C.2 From spatial texture to angular frequency

Assume the diffuse texture on the true surface contains a sinusoidal component along the tangential coordinate uu:

T⁡(u)⊃a​sin⁡(k​u),a>0,k>0,T(u)\ \supset\ a\sin(ku),\qquad a>0,\ k>0,

as in the texture assumption in the main paper. The through-seen target seen at the fake point x0x_{0} (ignoring other terms for the moment) includes

a​sin⁡(k​xhit​(α))=a​sin⁡(k⁡(x0+Δ​z​tan⁡α)).a\sin\big(k\,x_{\mathrm{hit}}(\alpha)\big)=a\sin\!\big(k(x_{0}+\Delta z\tan\alpha)\big).

On a moderate angular range where |α||\alpha| stays bounded away from π/2\pi/2, we may locally linearize tan⁡α≈α\tan\alpha\approx\alpha, yielding

a​sin⁡(k​x0+(k​Δ​z)​α),a\sin\!\big(kx_{0}+(k\Delta z)\alpha\big),

which is a sinusoid in the angular variable α\alpha with angular frequency

ωfake≈k​Δ​z,\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}\ \approx\ k\Delta z,

as stated in the induced-frequency relation in the main paper. This computation is local, and therefore applies to general smooth surfaces by restricting to a sufficiently small patch and a sufficiently small viewing arc where the planar approximation is valid.

0.C.3 Proof of the great-circle bandlimit lemma

Here we prove the great-circle bandlimit lemma in the main paper.

Let h∈𝒱Lh\in\mathcal{V}_{L}, so

h⁡(v^)=∑ℓ=0L∑m=−ℓℓcℓ​m​Yℓ​m​(v^).h(\hat{v})=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}c_{\ell m}Y_{\ell m}(\hat{v}).

Because 𝒱L\mathcal{V}_{L} is rotation-invariant, it suffices to prove the claim for the equator θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2 (any great circle can be rotated to the equator, and rotation preserves degree).

Write v^\hat{v} in spherical coordinates (θ,φ)(\theta,\varphi). For the standard complex SH basis,

Yℓ​m​(θ,φ)=Nℓ​m​Pℓm​(cos⁡θ)​ei​m​φ,Y_{\ell m}(\theta,\varphi)=N_{\ell m}\,P_{\ell}^{m}(\cos\theta)\,e^{im\varphi},

so restricting to the equator (θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2, cos⁡θ=0\cos\theta=0) yields

Yℓ​m​(π2,φ)=Nℓ​m​Pℓm​(0)⏟a constant in ​φ​ei​m​φ.Y_{\ell m}\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2},\varphi\right)=\underbrace{N_{\ell m}\,P_{\ell}^{m}(0)}_{\text{a constant in }\varphi}\,e^{im\varphi}.

Therefore the restriction h~​(φ):=h​(π/2,φ)\tilde{h}(\varphi):=h(\pi/2,\varphi) has the form

h~​(φ)=∑ℓ=0L∑m=−ℓℓc~ℓ​m​ei​m​φ=∑m=−LLdm​ei​m​φ,\tilde{h}(\varphi)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}\tilde{c}_{\ell m}\,e^{im\varphi}=\sum_{m=-L}^{L}d_{m}e^{im\varphi},

which is a trigonometric polynomial whose highest Fourier frequency is LL. The same conclusion holds for a real SH basis, since each real mode at order mm is a linear combination of cos⁡(m​φ)\cos(m\varphi) and sin⁡(m​φ)\sin(m\varphi).

0.C.4 Proof of the Fourier lower-bound lemma

Here we prove the Fourier lower-bound lemma in the main paper.

Consider the space of trigonometric polynomials of degree at most LL:

𝒯L:=span⁡{ei​m​φ:|m|≤L}⊂L2​([0,2​π]).\mathcal{T}_{L}:=\mathrm{span}\{e^{im\varphi}:\ |m|\leq L\}\subset L^{2}([0,2\pi]).

Let f⁡(φ)=a​sin⁡(ω​φ)f(\varphi)=a\sin(\omega\varphi) with a≠0a\neq 0 and integer ω\omega. Using

sin⁡(ω​φ)=ei​ω​φ−e−i​ω​φ2​i,\sin(\omega\varphi)=\frac{e^{i\omega\varphi}-e^{-i\omega\varphi}}{2i},

we see ff lives entirely in the frequency modes ±ω\pm\omega. If ω>L\omega>L, then ff is orthogonal to all basis functions ei​m​φe^{im\varphi} with |m|≤L|m|\leq L, hence orthogonal to the entire subspace 𝒯L\mathcal{T}_{L}. Therefore its orthogonal projection onto 𝒯L\mathcal{T}_{L} is the zero function, and the best approximation error equals its own energy:

infp∈𝒯L‖f−p‖L2​([0,2​π])2=‖f‖L2​([0,2​π])2=∫02​πa2​sin2⁡(ω​φ)​𝑑φ=a2​π.\inf_{p\in\mathcal{T}_{L}}\ \|f-p\|_{L^{2}([0,2\pi])}^{2}=\|f\|_{L^{2}([0,2\pi])}^{2}=\int_{0}^{2\pi}a^{2}\sin^{2}(\omega\varphi)\,d\varphi=a^{2}\pi.

This proves the Fourier lower-bound lemma in the main paper.

0.C.5 Robustness to additional terms (triangle inequality for distances to a subspace)

A simple inequality repeatedly used in the fake-geometry argument is:

dist(f+g,V)≥dist(f,V)−‖g‖,\dist(f+g,V)\ \geq\ \dist(f,V)\ -\ \|g\|, (21)

for any normed space, any subset VV, and any functions f,gf,g. Indeed, for any v∈Vv\in V,

‖f+g−v‖≥‖f−v‖−‖g‖,\|f+g-v\|\geq\|f-v\|-\|g\|,

and taking the infimum over v∈Vv\in V yields (21).

In our setting, ff is the transported high-frequency component from the diffuse texture, and gg collects all remaining terms (including the residual RR and other texture frequencies). Under the residual-amplitude assumption in the main paper, the gg term cannot completely cancel the amplitude of ff on the relevant set of rays, so the constant-scale lower bound survives.

0.C.6 From pointwise lower bounds to a global wrong-surface lower bound

To connect the 1D Fourier lower bound to BU​(L)B_{U}(L) in the misaligned-surface lower-bound proposition in the main paper, one uses:

  • •

    The pointwise projection characterization from the pointwise projection proposition in the main paper, which reduces BU​(L)B_{U}(L) to an average of pointwise squared distances dist(FU​(x,⋅),𝒱L)2\dist(F_{U}(x,\cdot),\mathcal{V}_{L})^{2} under μU\mu_{U}.

  • •

    The parallax computation above, which exhibits (on a visible patch with nonzero probability) a great-circle restriction of FU​(x,⋅)F_{U}(x,\cdot) containing a sinusoid at frequency ωfake≍k​Δ​z\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}\asymp k\Delta z (modulo the mild-angle approximation).

  • •

    The bandlimit lemma the great-circle bandlimit lemma in the main paper, implying any g⁡(x,⋅)∈𝒱Lg(x,\cdot)\in\mathcal{V}_{L} restricts to a trigonometric polynomial of degree at most LL on that viewing circle.

  • •

    The Fourier lower bound the Fourier lower-bound lemma in the main paper, implying an unavoidable constant residual whenever L<ωfakeL<\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}, which yields a strictly positive lower bound on dist(FU​(x,⋅),𝒱L)2\dist(F_{U}(x,\cdot),\mathcal{V}_{L})^{2} for those xx and directions.

Finally, since the ray distribution ℙ\mathbb{P} assigns positive probability mass to that visible patch (the texture assumption in the main paper and the misalignment assumption in the main paper), the global expectation defining BU​(L)B_{U}(L) inherits a strictly positive constant lower bound c0>0c_{0}>0 for all L<ωfakeL<\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}, completing the derivation behind the misaligned-surface lower-bound proposition in the main paper.

Appendix 0.D Numeric Example for the Scale Law

To make the threshold ωfake≈k​Δ​z\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}\approx k\Delta z tangible, consider a scene featuring a brick wall with grout lines spaced p=5p=5mm (0.0050.005m) apart. The spatial angular frequency of this texture component is:

k=2​πp≈2​π0.005≈1256​rad/m.k=\frac{2\pi}{p}\approx\frac{2\pi}{0.005}\approx 1256\ \text{rad/m}.

If the optimizer attempts to place a floater just 55cm (0.050.05m) in front of this wall, the parallax effect demands an induced angular frequency of:

ωfake≈k​Δ​z≈1256×0.05≈62.8.\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}\approx k\Delta z\approx 1256\times 0.05\approx 62.8.

To fake this specific geometry, the wrong surface must express angular variations on the order of frequency 6060. In stark contrast, the true surface does not need to convert this spatial texture into an angular signal at all; it merely needs to fit the residual RR, which is typically much smoother.

This calculation is not intended to establish L=60L=60 as a universal threshold. Rather, it illustrates the severe scaling dynamics of the ωfake\omega_{\mathrm{fake}} requirement. Fine textures combined with even modest geometric misalignments easily push the required angular frequency far beyond typical low SH degrees (e.g., L=2L=2 or 33), creating a robust and highly practical intermediate window where the true geometry is uniquely identifiable.

Appendix 0.E Large-LL Achievability: Billboards Can Match the Data

This appendix complements the lower bound in Appendix 0.C by showing that once the angular capacity exceeds the parallax-induced frequency ωfake\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}, a misaligned opaque billboard can fit the same images with equally low (indeed, zero) population loss under the first-hit model.

0.E.1 An idealized linear-parallax billboard setup

We work in the same 2D cross-section as Appendix 0.C. Let the true surface be the line S={z=zgt}S=\{z=z_{\mathrm{gt}}\} and the candidate billboard be the line U={z=zfake}U=\{z=z_{\mathrm{fake}}\} with depth gap Δ​z:=zgt−zfake>0\Delta z:=z_{\mathrm{gt}}-z_{\mathrm{fake}}>0.

Assume the ground-truth appearance is purely diffuse with a single spatial Fourier mode along the tangential coordinate:

B⁡(x,v^)=T⁡(x)=a​sin⁡(k​x),a>0,k>0.B(x,\hat{v})=T(x)=a\sin(kx),\qquad a>0,\ k>0. (22)

(Thus A⁡(L)=0A(L)=0 for all L≥0L\geq 0 since TT is view-independent.)

Fix a point x0x_{0} on the billboard UU. Let the set of training rays that hit x0x_{0} on UU arrive from a one-parameter family of viewing directions lying on a great circle, parameterized by an angle φ∈[0,2​π]\varphi\in[0,2\pi]. On this family we use the same linearized parallax relation as in the main text, i.e. we replace tan⁡(⋅)\tan(\cdot) by its first-order approximation:

xhit​(φ)=x0+Δ​z​φ.x_{\mathrm{hit}}(\varphi)=x_{0}+\Delta z\,\varphi. (23)

Therefore the through-seen target at the billboard point x0x_{0} is

FU​(x0,φ)=T⁡(xhit​(φ))=a​sin⁡(k​x0+(k​Δ​z)​φ).F_{U}(x_{0},\varphi)=T\!\left(x_{\mathrm{hit}}(\varphi)\right)=a\sin\!\big(kx_{0}+(k\Delta z)\varphi\big). (24)

Define the induced angular frequency

ωfake:=k​Δ​z.\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}:=k\Delta z. (25)

0.E.2 A surjectivity lemma: degree-LL SH can realize any degree-LL trigonometric polynomial on a great circle

Lemma 4 (Realizing trigonometric polynomials on a great circle)

Let CC be any great circle on 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2} with arc-length parameter φ∈[0,2​π]\varphi\in[0,2\pi]. For any trigonometric polynomial p⁡(φ)=∑m=−LLdm​ei​m​φp(\varphi)=\sum_{m=-L}^{L}d_{m}e^{im\varphi}, there exists a spherical harmonic polynomial h∈𝒱Lh\in\mathcal{V}_{L} such that hh restricted to CC equals pp: h|C​(φ)=p⁡(φ)h|_{C}(\varphi)=p(\varphi) for all φ\varphi.

Proof

By rotation invariance of 𝒱L\mathcal{V}_{L}, it suffices to treat the equator C={(θ,φ):θ=π/2}C=\{(\theta,\varphi):\theta=\pi/2\}. For the complex SH basis, Yℓ​m​(θ,φ)=Nℓ​m​Pℓm​(cos⁡θ)​ei​m​φY_{\ell m}(\theta,\varphi)=N_{\ell m}P_{\ell}^{m}(\cos\theta)e^{im\varphi}. Restricting to θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2 gives Yℓ​m​(π/2,φ)=Nℓ​m​Pℓm​(0)​ei​m​φY_{\ell m}(\pi/2,\varphi)=N_{\ell m}P_{\ell}^{m}(0)e^{im\varphi}. For each integer mm with |m|≤L|m|\leq L, take ℓ=|m|\ell=|m|. Then P|m||m|​(0)=(−1)|m|​(2​|m|−1)!!≠0P_{|m|}^{|m|}(0)=(-1)^{|m|}(2|m|-1)!!\neq 0, hence Y|m|,m​(π/2,φ)=cm​ei​m​φY_{|m|,m}(\pi/2,\varphi)=c_{m}e^{im\varphi} with cm≠0c_{m}\neq 0. Therefore, setting h⁡(v^)=∑m=−LL(dm/cm)​Y|m|,m​(v^)h(\hat{v})=\sum_{m=-L}^{L}(d_{m}/c_{m})\,Y_{|m|,m}(\hat{v}) yields h∈𝒱Lh\in\mathcal{V}_{L} and h⁡(π/2,φ)=p⁡(φ)h(\pi/2,\varphi)=p(\varphi).

0.E.3 Exact achievability once L≥ωfakeL\geq\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}

Proposition 4 (Billboard achieves zero loss for large enough LL)

In the setup above, assume ωfake=k​Δ​z\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}=k\Delta z is an integer. Then for any angular capacity L≥ωfakeL\geq\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}, there exists an appearance function gg on the billboard UU with g⁡(x,⋅)∈𝒱Lg(x,\cdot)\in\mathcal{V}_{L} for all x∈Ux\in U such that the first-hit predictions match the ground truth almost surely:

IU,g​(Y,V^)=I∗​(Y,V^).I_{U,g}(Y,\hat{V})=I^{*}(Y,\hat{V}).

Consequently, the optimal population loss is zero:

BU​(L)=0.B_{U}(L)=0.

Since in the pure diffuse case A⁡(L)=0A(L)=0 for all LL, we have A⁡(L)=BU​(L)=0A(L)=B_{U}(L)=0 for all L≥ωfakeL\geq\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}.

Proof

Fix x0∈Ux_{0}\in U. By (24), the required angular signal at x0x_{0} is the trigonometric polynomial

FU​(x0,φ)=a​sin⁡(k​x0+ωfake​φ)=a​sin⁡(k​x0)​cos⁡(ωfake​φ)+a​cos⁡(k​x0)​sin⁡(ωfake​φ).F_{U}(x_{0},\varphi)=a\sin(kx_{0}+\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}\varphi)=a\sin(kx_{0})\cos(\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}\varphi)+a\cos(kx_{0})\sin(\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}\varphi).

This has degree ωfake\omega_{\mathrm{fake}} in φ\varphi. Since L≥ωfakeL\geq\omega_{\mathrm{fake}}, Lemma 4 implies there exists hx0∈𝒱Lh_{x_{0}}\in\mathcal{V}_{L} whose restriction to the viewing great circle equals FU​(x0,φ)F_{U}(x_{0},\varphi). Define g⁡(x0,v^):=hx0​(v^)g(x_{0},\hat{v}):=h_{x_{0}}(\hat{v}). Repeating this construction pointwise for each x∈Ux\in U yields a measurable g:U×𝕊2→ℝg:U\times\mathbb{S}^{2}\to\mathbb{R} with g⁡(x,⋅)∈𝒱Lg(x,\cdot)\in\mathcal{V}_{L}.

By construction, for every training ray that first hits x0x_{0} on UU with direction parameter φ\varphi, we have g⁡(x0,v^​(φ))=FU​(x0,φ)=I∗​(y,v^​(φ))g(x_{0},\hat{v}(\varphi))=F_{U}(x_{0},\varphi)=I^{*}(y,\hat{v}(\varphi)), hence |IU,g−I∗|2=0|I_{U,g}-I^{*}|^{2}=0 on that ray. Therefore the population MSE is zero, so BU​(L)=0B_{U}(L)=0.

Extension to multiple texture frequencies.

If T⁡(x)T(x) is a finite Fourier series T⁡(x)=∑j=1Jaj​sin⁡(kj​x+ϕj)T(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{J}a_{j}\sin(k_{j}x+\phi_{j}), then the same proof shows BU​(L)=0B_{U}(L)=0 provided L≥maxj⁡(kj​Δ​z)L\geq\max_{j}(k_{j}\Delta z) (integer frequencies).

Appendix 0.F Experimental Details and Protocols

In this section, we provide the experimental protocols, evaluation metrics, and categorization criteria omitted from the main text due to space constraints.

0.F.1 Training Setup and Optimization

Across all synthetic and real-world experiments, we use the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization pipeline. We keep the core optimization schedules, including densification intervals, opacity reset frequencies, and learning-rate decays, at their default values. The independent variable in our ablation is the maximum spherical-harmonics degree LL, which we vary up to 2424. For high-capacity runs, the SH coefficients are optimized together with geometry to test whether the model uses excess angular capacity to fit appearance while leaving the true surface.

0.F.2 Geometric Evaluation and Normalization

We convert learned Gaussians into a point cloud by extracting their 3D centers. We first apply a similarity alignment (Umeyama algorithm) for global scale and rotation, followed by ICP alignment to the ground-truth mesh. We then sample 10510^{5} points from the aligned Gaussian centers and 10510^{5} points from the ground-truth surface.

To reduce sensitivity to distant floaters, we compute bidirectional point-to-point distances and truncate at the 99th percentile. We report normalized symmetric Chamfer distance,

nCD=CDdiag​(bbox​(GT)),\text{nCD}=\frac{\text{CD}}{\text{diag}(\text{bbox}(\text{GT}))},

where lower nCD indicates that Gaussian centers lie closer to the true surface.

0.F.3 Billboard Labeling Criterion

For each object, we identify the best appearance and geometry across all runs, denoted PSNRbest\text{PSNR}_{\text{best}} and nCDbest\text{nCD}_{\text{best}}. We classify each run as follows.

Opaque billboard.

The run has near-optimal rendering quality,

PSNR≥PSNRbest−2​dB,\text{PSNR}\geq\text{PSNR}_{\text{best}}-2\ \mathrm{dB},

but severely degraded geometry,

nCD≥5×nCDbest.\text{nCD}\geq 5\times\text{nCD}_{\text{best}}.

Billboard onset.

The run maintains near-optimal rendering quality but has moderate geometric drift:

2×nCDbest<nCD<5×nCDbest.2\times\text{nCD}_{\text{best}}<\text{nCD}<5\times\text{nCD}_{\text{best}}.

Surface-consistent.

The run remains geometrically stable, with nCD≤2×nCDbest\text{nCD}\leq 2\times\text{nCD}_{\text{best}}.
